newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sigma sees insurance growth in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Sigma sees insurance growth in Latin America.

text.p: Latin America offers insurers a competitive but promising growth market as reforms continue to bolster the region's economies, according to Sigma, the research bulletin of reinsurer Swiss Re.
Sigma's latest issues said Latin America was underdeveloped as an insurance market, with only 1.5 percent of global market share but eight percent of the world's population.
But it said the insurance industry had undergone a profound structural change since the end of the 1980s caused by broad economic liberalisation, sharply lower inflation and resulting growth.

"This also stimulated demand for insurance cover," Sigma said in a study of six countries that accounted for 90 percent of the region's 1995 premium volume of $30 billion -- Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Venzuela.
"In the medium to long-term, the prospects for growth in Latin America are still good," it said.

"Assuming that real gross domestic product (GDP) increases by 4-5 percent per annum by the end of the millenium, non-life insurance should grow by 6-8 percent real per annum on average and life insurance by over 10 percent," Sigma said.
It said this was twice the rate of that in the industrialised countries.

Wider economic reforms since the late 1980s meant insurance markets had also been largely deregulated and opened up to foreign insurers, although some restrictions still existed in Venezuela and Brazil.
"The high level of interest from foreign insurers and the ease of access to the market mean that competition will remain intense," the report said.
It said the exception as far as growth was Venezuela, where economic instability in the past five years had had an extremely negative effect on the insurance industry.

After growing an average 5.8 percent a year in the early 1990s, real premium volume for the region fell 1.6 percent in 1995 as the Mexican currency crisis and Argentine economic toubles added to the negative influence from Venezuela.
"The most stable development, with the highest rates of growth since 1980, was seen in Chile and Columbia," it said.
Sigma said insurance was still a fairly insignificant industry in Latin America, with the percentage of income spent on insurance in 1995 ranging from 1.5 percent in Mexico to 3.1 percent in Chile.
Non-life insurance clearly dominates the sector, with the most important non-life class of business in motor insurance,

Life insurance accounts for only 23 percent of premiums in Latin America, as against a worldwide average of 58 percent. But Sigma said the mix varied widely, between 2.5 percent and 50 percent among Latin American countries, and social security reforms should drive demand.
